newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian authorities warn opposition over protests.
newsitem.headline: Serbian authorities warn opposition over protests.

text.p: Police warned Serbia's opposition on Sunday against staging further street demonstrations which contain "elements of violence and serious violations of the law", state media reported.

The state news agency Tanjug quoted a statement from Belgrade police authorities saying they had been far too tolerant and would now hold organisers and parties responsible for any protests which violated the law.
The warning follows a two-week wave of street protests against Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic that have swept the capital and other major cities and towns.
The demonstrations were sparked by the annulment of opposition victories in municipal polls on November 17.
The authorities have deployed hundreds of police officers in riot gear, but sofar the police have kept a low profile.
The police statement and a vitriolic attack broadcast on state television against the opposition coalition both signalled that Milosevic's patience was wearing thin.
A botched local election has breathed life into a dormant opposition and set off the biggest political rallies in five years, since Milosevic crushed protests in 1991 with tanks and water-cannons.
The demonstrations have been mainly peaceful except for a few days in which protesters threw stones at state television and state newspaper offices, shattering windows.
Opposition stewards managed to put a stop to the stone throwing since Thursday and demonstrators since then have only hurled eggs, fruit and red paint bombs.
The police statement coincided with a condemnation of the opposition from the speaker of the parliament, Dragan Tomic, who is also a member of the ruling socialist party.
Speaking on state television news, Tomic branded the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition a "fascist" movement.
"These are not quiet demonstrations as the organisers presented them. These are destructive, massive demonstrations, with all elements of pro-fascist grouping and ideologies."
"Fascist ideology was never satisfied with the democratic process, with democratic elections but always forcibly came to power," he said.
State television showed footage of demonstrators throwing stones at plate glass windows in the building housing the state newspaper Politika earlier this week.
It also broadcast comments made earlier this month by the wife of an opposition leader, Vuk Draskovic.
Asked if it was time to form terrorist groups, Danica Draskovic, told reporters: "I can't wait for this to happen."
The opposition Zajedno coalition has tried to distance itself from Draskovic's comments and has been at pains to stress it wants peaceful, democratic change in Serbia.
Milosevic, who not yet made a public statement on the protests, has ruled the country with an iron hand since he rose to power as leader of the communist party nine years ago
